newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks enjoyed surprise party in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks enjoyed surprise party in 1996.

text.p: It was supposed to be the year the bull slowed to a crawl.
While the stock market's 1996 rally will not match 1995's, it came despite widespread predictions that inflation or weak corporate earnings would rain on Wall Street's parade.
Instead, every threat evaporated and the bulls staged what may have been their most satisfying and surprising run yet.
Entering 1996, analysts foresaw modest gains at best. After all, the Dow had surged a sizzling 33.5 percent in 1995 and faced major question marks in the economy and elections.
In the end, concerns about the political and economic environment were overdone, and the market celebrated the things that didn't happen.
While the bulls stumbled on the last day of trading of 1996, blue chips still rallied 1,331 points for the full year, a 26 percent climb.
The Dow, which was at 5,117.12 on Dec. 29, 1995, the last day of trading that year, closed out 1996 at 6,448.27 after falling 101.10 points in the year's last session on Tuesday.

"The surprise of 1996 was the economy was slower from a (gross domestic product) standpoint and more benign from an inflation standpoint than people expected," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer of Value Line Asset Management.

The year certainly had its bizarre moments. Early on, capital markets faced the odd spectacle of the shutdown of the U.S. government and late in the year global stock markets went into a tailspin over musings by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on the nature of "irrational exuberance."
Stock markets rallied despite a notable absence of the "January effect", the traditional rally in small-cap stocks.
And U.S. markets outpaced international markets despite widespread predictions to the contrary.
Ultimately, it was the friendly not-too-hot, not-too-cold U.S. economy that let financial markets thrive.
The atmosphere also eventually drained the suspense even from Wall Street's long-standing Fed-watching obsession.

"In 1996 there was constant attention on what the Fed would do and the Fed wound up doing very little," said Robert Stovall of Stovall/21st Securities. "Inflation was contained and the Fed had a remarkably long period of inactivity."

Indeed, the Fed has resisted changing rates since its first meeting of the year 11 months ago. The longest period of Fed inaction ever ran six months longer, ranging from September, 1992 to February 1994.
Which is not to say the road was without its bumps. A pair of sharp sell-offs exposed the market's vulnerability.
The most recent was the short-lived affair that followed Greenspan's rhetorical musings on the nature of "irrational exuberance."
The first was the market's severest trial over the last two years, one that began on what should have been a quiet, post-Independence Day session July 5.
Instead, a stunningly robust U.S. employment report roiled the bond market and dragged the Dow industrials down 114 points from their July 3 closing level of 5,703.
Blue chips shed 78 more points the next week and on Monday, July 15, the bottom fell out, as worries of soft corporate earnings linked with inflation fears to slam stocks.

The Dow tumbled 161 points on July 15 and another 160 points partway through July 16, leaving the average a full 500 points off its peak. But, just as suddenly, blue chips staged a ferocious recovery to end the session higher.
Though the inflation and earnings fears ultimately were proven unwarranted, the gyrations focused attention squarely on the increasingly powerful mutual funds.
"To me, this was the year of the intermediary," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer and Co. "The market was dominated by mutual fund portfolio managers."

For most of the year, cash inflows to funds fueled the market, producing a small-cap stock and initial public offering boom early in the year and the blue chip feeding frenzy of November. But at other times, investors showed themselves willing and able to withdraw, sharpening declines.
"That made the market very vulnerable to shifts in investor psychology," Metz said.
